items.title: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000
items.claim: In 2000, Netflix was a struggling DVD-by-mail service. What did Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco do when Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to propose a sale?

options.text: Agreed in principle but the deal collapsed over terms
Laughed Hastings out of the room
Counter-offered to buy Netflix for $200 million
Bought a minority stake to monitor the technology

items.reveal_title: The room where it didn't happen
items.reveal:
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph have both told the story (Randolph's book 'That Will Never Work' has the most colour). They proposed Blockbuster acquire Netflix for $50 million and run blockbuster.com as the online arm. Antioco — facing a profitable late-fee business model — declined.

Blockbuster did later launch an online service (Blockbuster Online) and was on a recovery path under Antioco, but a 2005 boardroom fight with activist investor Carl Icahn led to Antioco's departure and the strategy's reversal. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

Netflix's market cap is now over $300 billion.
items.why: Disruption isn't usually about technology incumbents can't access; it's about business models they can't bring themselves to attack. Late fees were too profitable to risk.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.
